free.q: A dose of 1.2 mg on a medicine chart is misread as 12 mg. How many times larger is the misread dose than the intended dose? Write your answer as a whole number.
free.w: Divide the misread dose by the intended dose: 12 mg / 1.2 mg = 10. Moving the decimal point one place to the right makes a number ten times larger, which is why a misplaced point is called a tenfold error. Sense check: 1.2 x 10 = 12. Type: 10

free.q: A 5 mL syringe is graduated every 0.2 mL, with a number at each whole mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the third small mark above 2. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.2 mL (five marks per whole mL). Step 2, count up from 2: three marks x 0.2 mL = 0.6 mL, so 2 + 0.6 = 2.6 mL. Sense check: the reading sits between 2 and 3 mL. Type: 2.6 mL

free.q: You have a prescription for 75 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
free.w: Tablets = dose wanted / strength of one tablet = 75 mg / 25 mg = 3 tablets. Sense check: 3 x 25 mg = 75 mg. Type: 3

free.q: A person is prescribed 200 mg of an oral suspension. The bottle label reads 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 200 mg / 250 mg x 5 mL = 0.8 x 5 = 4 mL. Sense check: 200 mg is a bit less than 250 mg, so a bit less than 5 mL. Typed answer: 4 mL

free.q: A person is prescribed morphine sulfate 5 mg by intramuscular injection. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 5 mg / 10 mg x 1 mL = 0.5 mL. Sense check: 5 mg is half of the 10 mg in the ampoule, so half of 1 mL. Type: 0.5 mL

free.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 8 hours, start 0800. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
free.w: Rate = volume / time = 1000 mL / 8 hours = 125 mL per hour. Sense check: 1000 mL over about 8 hours is a little over 100 mL each hour. Type: 125

free.q: A person's 24-hour fluid balance chart shows the following. Oral: 0700 200 mL, 1000 150 mL, 1300 250 mL, 1700 200 mL, 2100 120 mL. Urine: 0600 300 mL, 1100 250 mL, 1600 350 mL, 2200 280 mL. Vomit: 0900 90 mL. What is the fluid balance for the 24 hours? If the balance is a gain, put + before your answer (for example +100 mL). If it is a loss, put - before your answer (for example -100 mL). Please use the correct unit.
free.w: Total input: oral 200 + 150 + 250 + 200 + 120 = 920 mL. Total output: urine 300 + 250 + 350 + 280 = 1180 mL, plus vomit 90 mL = 1270 mL. Balance = input - output = 920 - 1270 = -350 mL. Sense check: output is bigger than input, so the balance is a loss and carries a minus sign. Type: -350 mL

free.q: You have a prescription for 40 mg. The ampoule label reads 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 40 / 100 x 2 = 0.8 mL. The value is below 1, so it needs a leading zero: 0.8 mL, not .8 mL, which Pearson marked wrong on the practice test. Sense check: 40 mg is under half of 100 mg, so under 1 mL. Type: 0.8 mL

free.q: A volume of 0.6 mL is needed but 6 mL has been drawn up in error. By how many millilitres is the drawn-up volume too large? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Subtract the intended volume from the volume drawn up: 6 mL - 0.6 mL = 5.4 mL. Line up the decimal points: 6.0 - 0.6 = 5.4. Sense check: 6 mL is ten times 0.6 mL, so the error is a little under 6 mL. Type: 5.4 mL

free.q: A 10 mL syringe has a small mark every 0.5 mL and a number at each whole mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the first small mark above 7. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.5 mL (one mark between whole numbers). Step 2, one mark above 7: 7 + 0.5 = 7.5 mL. Sense check: the reading is halfway between 7 and 8 mL. Type: 7.5 mL

free.q: A person is prescribed 30 mg of a medicine. Each tablet contains 7.5 mg. How many tablets should be given?
free.w: Tablets = want / have = 30 mg / 7.5 mg = 4 tablets. Sense check: 7.5 mg doubled is 15 mg, doubled again is 30 mg, so 4 tablets. Type: 4

free.q: You have a prescription for 15 mg of an oral solution. The label reads 5 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 15 mg / 5 mg x 1 mL = 3 mL. Sense check: each mL holds 5 mg, so 3 mL holds 15 mg. Typed answer: 3 mL

free.q: A person is prescribed gentamicin 60 mg by slow intravenous injection. The vial label reads 80 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 60 mg / 80 mg x 2 mL = 0.75 x 2 = 1.5 mL. Sense check: 60 mg is three quarters of the 80 mg in the vial, so three quarters of 2 mL. Type: 1.5 mL

free.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 500 mL, IV, over 5 hours, start 1000. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
free.w: Rate = volume / time = 500 mL / 5 hours = 100 mL per hour. Sense check: 100 mL each hour for 5 hours is 500 mL. Type: 100

free.q: A person's 24-hour fluid balance chart shows the following. Oral: 0800 250 mL, 1100 200 mL, 1400 150 mL, 1800 300 mL, 2200 100 mL. Intravenous: 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL given 1000 to 1400, recorded as 500 mL at 1400. Urine: 0600 400 mL, 1200 350 mL, 1900 450 mL. What is the total input for the 24 hours?
free.w: Input is everything going in: oral 250 + 200 + 150 + 300 + 100 = 1000 mL, plus the 500 mL intravenous bag = 1500 mL. Urine is output, so it is not added. Sense check: about 1 L by mouth plus half a litre IV is about 1.5 L. Type: 1500

free.q: You have a prescription for 250 mg. The bottle label reads 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 250 / 125 x 5 = 2 x 5 = 10 mL. The answer is whole, so type it with no decimal point and no trailing zero, then the unit: 10 mL, not 10.0 mL or 10 mls. Type: 10 mL

free.q: Each millilitre of a solution contains 0.04 g. How many grams are in 10 mL? Write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Multiply the amount in 1 mL by the number of millilitres: 0.04 g x 10 = 0.4 g. Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the right: 0.04 becomes 0.4. Sense check: 10 lots of a small amount is still less than 1 g. Type: 0.4

free.q: A 1 mL syringe is graduated every 0.01 mL, with a number at every 0.1 mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the seventh small mark above 0.3. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
free.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.01 mL (ten marks per 0.1 mL). Step 2, seven marks above 0.3: 7 x 0.01 = 0.07, so 0.3 + 0.07 = 0.37 mL. Keep the leading zero. Type: 0.37 mL

free.q: A person is prescribed prednisolone 20 mg. The stock tablets contain 5 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
free.w: Tablets = want / have = 20 mg / 5 mg = 4 tablets. Sense check: 4 x 5 mg = 20 mg, and 4 tablets is a realistic number to give. Type: 4

free.q: A person is prescribed 125 mg of an oral solution. The label reads 50 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 125 mg / 50 mg x 5 mL = 2.5 x 5 = 12.5 mL. Sense check: 125 mg is two and a half times 50 mg, so two and a half times 5 mL. Typed answer: 12.5 mL

free.q: A person is prescribed morphine sulfate 2.5 mg by subcutaneous injection. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 2.5 mg / 10 mg x 1 mL = 0.25 mL. Sense check: 2.5 mg is a quarter of 10 mg, so a quarter of 1 mL. Type: 0.25 mL

free.q: Prescription: Hartmann's solution (compound sodium lactate), 1000 mL, IV, over 5 hours, start 0600. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
free.w: Rate = volume / time = 1000 mL / 5 hours = 200 mL per hour. Sense check: 200 mL each hour for 5 hours is 1000 mL. Type: 200

free.q: A person's 24-hour fluid balance chart shows the following. Oral: 0700 200 mL, 1200 250 mL, 1800 200 mL. Urine: 0500 400 mL, 1000 350 mL, 1500 300 mL, 2000 250 mL, 2300 200 mL. Wound drain: 0800 80 mL, 1600 60 mL. What is the total output for the 24 hours?
free.w: Output is everything coming out: urine 400 + 350 + 300 + 250 + 200 = 1500 mL, plus wound drain 80 + 60 = 140 mL, total 1640 mL. Oral fluid is input and is not counted here. Sense check: 1.5 L of urine plus a small drain loss is just over 1.6 L. Type: 1640

free.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 900 mL, IV, over 6 hours, start 0800. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
free.w: Rate = volume / time = 900 mL / 6 hours = 150 mL per hour. The box is number-only with "mL per hour" printed after it, so type the number alone: no unit, no words. Type: 150

free.q: A dose of 0.125 mg is written on a prescription. How many micrograms is this?
free.w: Milligrams to micrograms: multiply by 1,000 (1 mg = 1,000 micrograms). 0.125 x 1,000 = 125 micrograms; the decimal point moves three places to the right. Sense check: a fraction of a milligram is a few hundred micrograms at most. Type: 125

free.q: A 2 mL syringe is graduated every 0.1 mL, with a number at every 0.5 mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the fourth small mark above 1.5. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.1 mL (five marks between numbers 0.5 mL apart). Step 2, four marks above 1.5: 4 x 0.1 = 0.4, so 1.5 + 0.4 = 1.9 mL. Sense check: just under 2 mL. Type: 1.9 mL

free.q: You have a prescription for 2.5 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 1.25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
free.w: Tablets = want / have = 2.5 mg / 1.25 mg = 2 tablets. Sense check: 1.25 mg + 1.25 mg = 2.5 mg. The decimals do not change the method. Type: 2

free.q: A person is prescribed 300 mg of an oral suspension. The label reads 400 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 300 mg / 400 mg x 5 mL = 0.75 x 5 = 3.75 mL. Round to one decimal place: 3.75 becomes 3.8 mL (5 rounds up). Typed answer: 3.8 mL

free.q: A person is prescribed dexamethasone 6.6 mg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 3.3 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
free.w: Want / have x volume = 6.6 mg / 3.3 mg x 1 mL = 2 x 1 mL = 2 mL. Sense check: the dose is exactly twice the amount in 1 mL. Type: 2 mL

free.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 250 mL, IV, over 30 minutes, start 1400. At what rate should the infusion pump be set, in mL per hour?
free.w: Change minutes to hours by multiplying by 60: rate = volume / minutes x 60 = 250 mL / 30 x 60 = 500 mL per hour. Sense check: an hour is 2 lots of 30 minutes, so the hourly rate is 2 x 250 mL. Type: 500

free.q: A person's 24-hour fluid balance chart shows the following. Oral: 0700 300 mL, 1000 200 mL, 1200 250 mL, 1500 200 mL, 1800 300 mL, 2100 150 mL. Intravenous (bag completed): 0900 500 mL, 2100 500 mL. Urine: 0600 450 mL, 1100 400 mL, 1600 500 mL, 2200 450 mL. What is the fluid balance for the 24 hours? If the balance is a gain, put + before your answer (for example +100 mL). If it is a loss, put - before your answer (for example -100 mL). Please use the correct unit.
free.w: Total input: oral 300 + 200 + 250 + 200 + 300 + 150 = 1400 mL, plus IV 500 + 500 = 1000 mL, total 2400 mL. Total output: urine 450 + 400 + 500 + 450 = 1800 mL. Balance = 2400 - 1800 = +600 mL. Sense check: more went in than came out, so it is a gain with a plus sign. Type: +600 mL

free.q: A person is advised to drink 2.5 L of fluid a day. What is this volume in mL?
free.w: L to mL: multiply by 1000. 2.5 x 1000 = 2500 mL. Type it without a thousands comma: the number-only box rejects "2,500". Sense check: 2.5 L is two and a half litres, so two and a half thousand mL. Type: 2500

paid.q: A 100 mL bottle contains 4.5 g of a medicine evenly mixed through the liquid. How many milligrams of the medicine are in 1 mL?
paid.w: Step 1, grams to milligrams: 4.5 g x 1,000 = 4,500 mg. Step 2, share across 100 mL: 4,500 mg / 100 = 45 mg in each mL. Sense check: 45 mg x 100 mL = 4,500 mg = 4.5 g. Type: 45

paid.q: A solution contains 2.5 mg in each 1 mL. How many milligrams are in 10 mL?
paid.w: Multiply the amount per mL by the volume: 2.5 mg x 10 = 25 mg. Multiplying by 10 moves the point one place right: 2.5 becomes 25. Sense check: 10 mL holds ten times as much as 1 mL. Type: 25

paid.q: A total of 7.5 mg is shared equally between 10 doses. How many milligrams are in each dose? Write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Divide the total by the number of doses: 7.5 mg / 10 = 0.75 mg. Dividing by 10 moves the point one place to the left, and a zero goes in front of the point. Sense check: each dose must be smaller than 1 mg because 10 x 1 mg would be 10 mg. Type: 0.75

paid.q: A pack holds 100 sachets, each containing 0.05 g of powder. How many grams of powder are in the whole pack?
paid.w: Multiply the amount in one sachet by the number of sachets: 0.05 g x 100 = 5 g. Multiplying by 100 moves the point two places to the right: 0.05 becomes 5. Sense check: 0.05 is one twentieth, and one twentieth of 100 is 5. Type: 5

paid.q: A person was meant to receive 0.2 mg but was given 2 mg. How many milligrams more than intended were given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Subtract the intended dose from the dose given: 2 mg - 0.2 mg = 1.8 mg. Line up the points: 2.0 - 0.2 = 1.8. Sense check: 2 mg is ten times 0.2 mg, so the extra amount is nine times the intended dose (9 x 0.2 = 1.8). Type: 1.8 mg

paid.q: A solution containing 0.5 mg in 1 mL is diluted so that each 1 mL contains one tenth of that amount. How many micrograms are in each 1 mL of the diluted solution?
paid.w: Step 1, one tenth of 0.5 mg: 0.5 / 10 = 0.05 mg in each mL. Step 2, milligrams to micrograms: 0.05 x 1,000 = 50 micrograms. Sense check: 0.5 mg is 500 micrograms, and one tenth of 500 is 50. Type: 50

paid.q: Convert 2.5 g to milligrams.
paid.w: Grams to milligrams: multiply by 1,000 because 1 g = 1,000 mg. 2.5 x 1,000 = 2,500 mg (move the point three places right). Type the number without a comma, as the number-only box rejects commas. Type: 2500

paid.q: Convert 750 micrograms to milligrams. Write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Micrograms to milligrams: divide by 1,000 because 1 mg = 1,000 micrograms. 750 / 1,000 = 0.75 mg (move the point three places left and add a leading zero). Sense check: 750 micrograms is less than 1,000 micrograms, so less than 1 mg. Type: 0.75

paid.q: Convert 0.4 mg to micrograms.
paid.w: Milligrams to micrograms: multiply by 1,000. 0.4 x 1,000 = 400 micrograms. Sense check: 1 mg is 1,000 micrograms, so a bit less than half a milligram is a bit less than 500 micrograms. Type: 400

paid.q: Convert 1500 mg to grams. Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Milligrams to grams: divide by 1,000 because 1 g = 1,000 mg. 1,500 / 1,000 = 1.5 g. Sense check: 1,500 mg is one and a half thousand milligrams, so 1.5 g. Type the number and the unit: 1.5 g

paid.q: Convert 0.85 kg to grams.
paid.w: Kilograms to grams: multiply by 1,000 because 1 kg = 1,000 g. 0.85 x 1,000 = 850 g. Sense check: just under 1 kg is just under 1,000 g. Type: 850

paid.q: Convert 0.0625 mg to micrograms. Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Milligrams to micrograms: multiply by 1,000. 0.0625 x 1,000 = 62.5 micrograms (move the point three places right). The exact answer already has one decimal place. Sense check: a very small fraction of 1 mg is a small number of micrograms. Type: 62.5

paid.q: Convert 250 mg to grams. Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Milligrams to grams: divide by 1,000. 250 / 1,000 = 0.25 g; put a zero before the point. Sense check: 250 mg is a quarter of 1,000 mg, so a quarter of a gram. Type: 0.25 g

paid.q: Convert 0.75 L to millilitres.
paid.w: Litres to millilitres: multiply by 1,000 because 1 L = 1,000 mL. 0.75 x 1,000 = 750 mL. Sense check: three quarters of a litre is three quarters of 1,000 mL. Type: 750

paid.q: Convert 1250 mL to litres. Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Millilitres to litres: divide by 1,000. 1,250 / 1,000 = 1.25 L. Sense check: 1,000 mL is 1 L, and the extra 250 mL is a quarter of a litre. Type the number and the unit: 1.25 L

paid.q: Convert 2.4 L to millilitres.
paid.w: Litres to millilitres: multiply by 1,000. 2.4 x 1,000 = 2,400 mL. Type it without a comma. Sense check: a little under two and a half litres is a little under 2,500 mL. Type: 2400

paid.q: Convert 350 mL to litres. Write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Millilitres to litres: divide by 1,000. 350 / 1,000 = 0.35 L, with a zero before the point. Sense check: 350 mL is about a third of a litre. Type: 0.35

paid.q: A bag holds 1 L of fluid. After 650 mL has been used, how many millilitres remain in the bag?
paid.w: Step 1, convert the bag to millilitres: 1 L = 1,000 mL. Step 2, subtract what has been used: 1,000 mL - 650 mL = 350 mL. Sense check: 650 mL is about two thirds of the bag, so about a third remains. Type: 350

paid.q: Drinks of 200 mL, 150 mL and 180 mL are taken over a morning. What is the total volume in litres? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Step 1, add the drinks: 200 + 150 + 180 = 530 mL. Step 2, millilitres to litres: 530 / 1,000 = 0.53 L. Sense check: just over half a litre. Type: 0.53 L

paid.q: A client drinks 0.45 L of juice with lunch. What is this volume in millilitres?
paid.w: Litres to millilitres: multiply by 1,000. 0.45 x 1,000 = 450 mL. Sense check: a little under half a litre is a little under 500 mL. Bigger unit to smaller unit means a bigger number. Type: 450

paid.q: A client's daily drink target is 1.8 L. They have drunk 1150 mL so far today. How many more millilitres do they need to drink to reach the target? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, convert the target to millilitres: 1.8 L x 1,000 = 1,800 mL. Step 2, subtract what has been drunk: 1,800 - 1,150 = 650 mL. Sense check: 1,150 + 650 = 1,800. Type: 650 mL

paid.q: In a residential home, a client drinks 275 mL, 300 mL and 425 mL during the morning. What is the total volume in litres?
paid.w: Step 1, add the drinks: 275 + 300 + 425 = 1,000 mL. Step 2, millilitres to litres: 1,000 / 1,000 = 1 L. The answer is a whole number, so type it with no decimal point or trailing zero. Type: 1

paid.q: A label reads potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1000 mL. How many millimoles are in 250 mL?
paid.w: Amount per mL x volume: 40 mmol / 1,000 mL x 250 mL = 10 mmol. Or: 250 mL is a quarter of 1,000 mL, so a quarter of 40 mmol = 10 mmol. Millimoles follow the same want/have arithmetic as milligrams. Type: 10

paid.q: A solution contains 20 mmol in 10 mL. How many millimoles are in 1 mL?
paid.w: Divide the amount by the volume: 20 mmol / 10 mL = 2 mmol in each mL. Sense check: 10 x 2 = 20. Millimoles use the same arithmetic as milligrams. Type: 2

paid.q: A vial is labelled 5,000 units in 1 mL. How many units are in 0.4 mL?
paid.w: Units per mL x volume: 5,000 units x 0.4 = 2,000 units. Type it with no comma. Sense check: 0.4 mL is less than half of 1 mL, so less than 2,500 units. Type: 2000

paid.q: Insulin in a pen device is labelled 100 units/mL. How many units are in 0.15 mL?
paid.w: Units per mL x volume: 100 units x 0.15 = 15 units. Sense check: 0.1 mL would be 10 units, so 0.15 mL is one and a half times that. Type: 15

paid.q: A bag contains potassium chloride 20 mmol in 500 mL. How many millimoles would 1 L of the same solution contain?
paid.w: Step 1, 1 L = 1,000 mL, which is twice 500 mL. Step 2, twice the amount: 20 mmol / 500 mL x 1,000 mL = 40 mmol. Type: 40

paid.q: Convert 2.5 hours to minutes.
paid.w: Hours to minutes: multiply by 60 because 1 hour = 60 minutes. 2.5 x 60 = 150 minutes. Time is not decimal: 2.5 hours is 2 hours 30 minutes, not 2 hours 50 minutes. Type: 150

paid.q: Convert 45 minutes to hours. Write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Minutes to hours: divide by 60. 45 / 60 = 0.75 hours (three quarters of an hour). Sense check: 30 minutes is 0.5 hours and 45 minutes is a bit more. Type: 0.75

paid.q: An infusion runs from 0815 to 1345 on the same day. For how many minutes does it run?
paid.w: Count in steps: 0815 to 1315 is 5 hours = 300 minutes; 1315 to 1345 is 30 minutes. Total 300 + 30 = 330 minutes. Subtracting the clock times as ordinary numbers (1345 - 815 = 530) is wrong because an hour has 60 minutes, not 100. Type: 330

paid.q: An infusion starts at 0930 and runs for 8 hours. At what time does it finish? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits (for example 1430).
paid.w: Add 8 hours to the start time: 09:30 + 8 hours = 17:30, written 1730 in the 24-hour clock. Sense check: half past nine in the morning plus 8 hours is half past five in the afternoon. Type: 1730

paid.q: A medicine is given every 6 hours. The first dose is given at 0600. At what time is the third dose due? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits (for example 1430).
paid.w: The third dose comes two intervals after the first: 0600, then 1200 (second dose), then 1800 (third dose). 6 + 2 x 6 = 18, so 1800. Count the doses, not the gaps. Type: 1800

paid.q: An infusion has run for 3 hours 20 minutes. How many minutes is this?
paid.w: Convert the whole hours first: 3 hours x 60 = 180 minutes. Then add the extra 20 minutes: 180 + 20 = 200 minutes. Sense check: 3 hours 20 minutes is a little over 3 hours, and 3 hours is 180 minutes. Type: 200

paid.q: A 90-minute infusion is followed straight away by a 45-minute infusion. What is the total time in hours? Write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Step 1, total minutes: 90 + 45 = 135 minutes. Step 2, minutes to hours: 135 / 60 = 2.25 hours (2 hours 15 minutes). Sense check: a little over 2 hours. Type: 2.25

paid.q: An infusion started at 2200 and stopped at 0430 the next morning. For how many hours did it run? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Count across midnight: 2200 to 2400 is 2 hours; 0000 to 0430 is 4 hours 30 minutes. Total 6 hours 30 minutes. Minutes to hours: 30 / 60 = 0.5, so 6.5 hours. Type: 6.5

paid.q: A bag of 5% w/v glucose contains 5 g of glucose in every 100 mL. How many grams of glucose are in a 500 mL bag?
paid.w: Per cent w/v means grams per 100 mL. 500 mL is 5 lots of 100 mL, so 5 g x 5 = 25 g. As a formula: 5 g / 100 mL x 500 mL = 25 g. Type: 25

paid.q: Sodium chloride 0.9% w/v contains 0.9 g in every 100 mL. How many grams of sodium chloride are in 1 L?
paid.w: Step 1, 1 L = 1,000 mL, which is 10 lots of 100 mL. Step 2, 0.9 g x 10 = 9 g. As a formula: 0.9 g / 100 mL x 1,000 mL = 9 g. Type: 9

paid.q: Adrenaline 1 in 1,000 means 1 g in 1,000 mL. How many milligrams are in 1 mL?
paid.w: Step 1, 1 g = 1,000 mg, so the solution has 1,000 mg in 1,000 mL. Step 2, per mL: 1,000 mg / 1,000 mL = 1 mg/mL. Type: 1

paid.q: A 10% w/v solution contains 10 g in every 100 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?
paid.w: Step 1, grams to milligrams: 10 g = 10,000 mg in 100 mL. Step 2, per mL: 10,000 mg / 100 mL = 100 mg/mL. Sense check: 100 mg x 100 mL = 10,000 mg = 10 g. Type: 100

paid.q: A 20 mL syringe is graduated every 1 mL, with a number at every 5 mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the third small mark above 15. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 1 mL (five marks per 5 mL). Step 2, three marks above 15: 15 + 3 = 18 mL. The answer is a whole number, so no decimal point. Type: 18 mL

paid.q: A 3 mL syringe is graduated every 0.1 mL, with a number at every 0.5 mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the second small mark above 2.5. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.1 mL. Step 2, two marks above 2.5: 2 x 0.1 = 0.2, so 2.5 + 0.2 = 2.7 mL. Sense check: between 2.5 and 3 mL. Type: 2.7 mL

paid.q: A 5 mL syringe is graduated every 0.2 mL, with a number at each whole mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the fourth small mark above zero. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.2 mL. Step 2, four marks above zero: 4 x 0.2 = 0.8 mL. Put a zero before the point: ".8 mL" was marked wrong on the Pearson practice test. Type: 0.8 mL

paid.q: A 10 mL syringe is graduated every 0.2 mL, with a number at each whole mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the second small mark above 4. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.2 mL (five marks per whole mL). Step 2, two marks above 4: 2 x 0.2 = 0.4, so 4 + 0.4 = 4.4 mL. Sense check: a little under halfway from 4 to 5 mL. Type: 4.4 mL

paid.q: A 10 mL syringe is graduated every 0.2 mL, with a number at each whole mL. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the second small mark below 9. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.2 mL. Step 2, two marks below 9: 2 x 0.2 = 0.4, so 9 - 0.4 = 8.6 mL. Sense check: between 8 and 9 mL, nearer 9. Type: 8.6 mL

paid.q: A client's medicine is drawn up in a 1 mL syringe graduated every 0.1 mL, with numbers at 0.5 and 1. The top of the plunger seal lines up with the second small mark above 0.5. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.1 mL (five marks per 0.5 mL). Step 2, two marks above 0.5: 2 x 0.1 = 0.2, so 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7 mL. Keep the leading zero. Type: 0.7 mL

paid.q: A client's oral liquid is measured in a 10 mL oral syringe graduated every 0.2 mL, with a number at each whole mL. The plunger seal lines up with the second small mark above 6. What volume has been drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each small mark: 0.2 mL (five marks per whole mL). Step 2, two marks above 6: 2 x 0.2 = 0.4, so 6 + 0.4 = 6.4 mL. Sense check: between 6 and 7 mL. Type: 6.4 mL

paid.q: A 30 mL medicine pot has a mark every 5 mL, with numbers at 10, 20 and 30. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark above 20. What volume has been dispensed? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each mark: 5 mL (one unnumbered mark between numbers 10 mL apart). Step 2, one mark above 20: 20 + 5 = 25 mL. Read at the bottom of the meniscus with the pot at eye level. Type: 25 mL

paid.q: A 30 mL medicine pot has a mark every 2.5 mL, with numbers at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark between 10 and 15. What volume has been dispensed? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each mark: 2.5 mL (one unnumbered mark halfway between numbers 5 mL apart). Step 2, 10 + 2.5 = 12.5 mL. Sense check: halfway between 10 and 15. Type: 12.5 mL

paid.q: A medicine pot is graduated every 2.5 mL up to 30 mL, with numbers every 5 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the first mark above 25. What volume is in the pot? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each mark: 2.5 mL. Step 2, one mark above 25: 25 + 2.5 = 27.5 mL. Sense check: between 25 and 30 mL. Type: 27.5 mL

paid.q: A 10 mL medicine pot is graduated every 2.5 mL, with numbers at 5 and 10. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark between 5 and 10. What volume is in the pot? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each mark: 2.5 mL (one mark halfway between 5 and 10). Step 2, 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 mL. Read at the bottom of the meniscus with the pot at eye level. Type: 7.5 mL

paid.q: A 30 mL medicine pot has a mark every 5 mL, with numbers at 10, 20 and 30. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark between 10 and 20. What volume has been poured? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each mark: 5 mL. Step 2, one mark above 10: 10 + 5 = 15 mL. Read at the bottom of the meniscus, with the pot on a flat surface at eye level. Sense check: halfway between 10 and 20. Type: 15 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 20 mL of an oral liquid. A 30 mL medicine pot graduated every 2.5 mL, with numbers every 5 mL, shows the liquid level with the first mark above 15. How many more millilitres must be poured? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, read the pot: one 2.5 mL mark above 15 = 17.5 mL. Step 2, subtract from the dose: 20 - 17.5 = 2.5 mL more to pour. Type: 2.5 mL

paid.q: A 60 mL oral measure has a mark every 5 mL, with numbers every 10 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark between 40 and 50. What volume is in the measure? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, value of each mark: 5 mL (one mark between numbers 10 mL apart). Step 2, 40 + 5 = 45 mL. Read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. Sense check: halfway between 40 and 50. Type: 45 mL

paid.q: A 5 mL syringe has 25 equal small divisions between 0 and 5 mL. What volume does each small division represent? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Divide the capacity by the number of divisions: 5 mL / 25 = 0.2 mL per division. Sense check: 5 divisions make 1 mL. Find this value first whenever a syringe scale is unfamiliar. Type: 0.2 mL

paid.q: A 1 mL syringe has 100 equal small divisions between 0 and 1 mL. What volume does each small division represent? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Divide the capacity by the number of divisions: 1 mL / 100 = 0.01 mL per division. This is why a 1 mL syringe measures small doses to two decimal places. Type: 0.01 mL

paid.q: A volume of 2.6 mL is to be measured in one draw. Syringes of 1 mL, 2 mL, 5 mL and 10 mL are available. What is the capacity of the smallest syringe that holds the whole volume? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Choose the smallest syringe that holds the whole volume in one draw: 1 mL and 2 mL are too small for 2.6 mL, so 5 mL is the smallest that fits. A smaller syringe has finer graduations and measures more accurately than 10 mL. Type: 5 mL

paid.q: A volume of 25 mL is to be given using a 10 mL oral syringe. What is the least number of times the syringe must be filled? Give your answer as a whole number.
paid.w: Divide the volume by the syringe capacity: 25 / 10 = 2.5 fills. A part-fill still needs a separate draw, so round up: 3 fills (10 mL + 10 mL + 5 mL). Type: 3

paid.q: A volume of 0.35 mL is to be measured in a 1 mL syringe graduated every 0.01 mL. How many small graduations above zero should the plunger seal reach?
paid.w: Divide the volume by the value of one graduation: 0.35 mL / 0.01 mL = 35 graduations. Sense check: 0.1 mL is 10 graduations, so 0.35 mL is 35. Type: 35

paid.q: A volume of 12 mL is to be measured in one draw. Syringes of 1 mL, 3 mL, 5 mL, 10 mL and 20 mL are available. What is the capacity of the smallest syringe that holds the whole volume? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: The syringe must hold all 12 mL in one draw: 10 mL is too small, so the smallest syringe that fits is 20 mL. Drawing up twice in a smaller syringe adds a measuring error. Type: 20 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 300 mg of an oral suspension. The stock strength is 150 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 300 mg / 150 mg x 5 mL = 2 x 5 = 10 mL. Sense check: the dose is twice the 150 mg in 5 mL, so twice 5 mL. Type: 10 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 45 mg. The ampoule contains 50 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 45 mg / 50 mg x 2 mL = 0.9 x 2 = 1.8 mL. Sense check: 45 mg is a little less than 50 mg, so a little less than 2 mL. Type: 1.8 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 2 mg of an oral solution. The stock strength is 5 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 2 mg / 5 mg x 5 mL = 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL. The stock is 1 mg in each mL, so 2 mg is 2 mL. Type: 2 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 125 mg of an oral suspension. The stock strength is 250 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 125 mg / 250 mg x 5 mL = 0.5 x 5 = 2.5 mL. Sense check: half the stock dose needs half of 5 mL. Type: 2.5 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 37.5 mg of an oral liquid. The stock strength is 25 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 37.5 mg / 25 mg x 5 mL = 1.5 x 5 = 7.5 mL. Sense check: one and a half times the 25 mg dose needs one and a half times 5 mL. Type: 7.5 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 40 mg by injection. The ampoule contains 60 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 40 mg / 60 mg x 1 mL = 0.6666... mL. Round to two decimal places: the third digit is 6, so round up to 0.67 mL. Sense check: two thirds of 1 mL. Type: 0.67 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 0.5 g of an oral suspension. The stock strength is 250 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, same units first: 0.5 g x 1,000 = 500 mg. Step 2, want / have x volume = 500 mg / 250 mg x 5 mL = 2 x 5 = 10 mL. Sense check: twice the stock dose, twice the volume. Type: 10 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 90 mg of an oral liquid. The stock strength is 40 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 90 mg / 40 mg x 5 mL = 2.25 x 5 = 11.25 mL. Round to one decimal place: the second digit is 5, so round up to 11.3 mL. Sense check: a bit more than twice 5 mL. Type: 11.3 mL

paid.q: A bottle label reads 250 mg/5 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: "250 mg/5 mL" means every 5 mL contains 250 mg. Divide the dose by the volume: 250 mg / 5 mL = 50 mg in each mL. Sense check: 50 mg x 5 = 250 mg. Type: 50 mg

paid.q: An ampoule label reads 100 mg/2 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: "100 mg/2 mL" means the whole 2 mL ampoule holds 100 mg, not 100 mg in each mL. Per mL: 100 mg / 2 mL = 50 mg. Misreading this label doubles the dose. Type: 50 mg

paid.q: An oral liquid label reads 120 mg/5 mL, and the bottle holds 100 mL. How many milligrams are in the full bottle? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, per mL: 120 mg / 5 mL = 24 mg in each mL. Step 2, whole bottle: 24 mg x 100 mL = 2,400 mg. Type without a comma. Sense check: 100 mL is 20 lots of 5 mL, and 20 x 120 = 2,400. Type: 2400 mg

paid.q: An ampoule label reads 10 mg in 2 mL. How many milligrams are in 0.5 mL? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, per mL: 10 mg / 2 mL = 5 mg in each mL. Step 2, 5 mg x 0.5 mL = 2.5 mg. Sense check: 0.5 mL is a quarter of the 2 mL ampoule, so a quarter of 10 mg. Type: 2.5 mg

paid.q: A label reads 1 g in 10 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Step 1, grams to milligrams: 1 g = 1,000 mg in 10 mL. Step 2, per mL: 1,000 mg / 10 mL = 100 mg. Sense check: 100 mg x 10 = 1,000 mg = 1 g. Type: 100 mg

paid.q: A 1 mL vial is labelled 500 micrograms in 1 mL. How many milligrams are in the vial? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Micrograms to milligrams: divide by 1,000. 500 micrograms / 1,000 = 0.5 mg, written with a leading zero. Smaller unit to bigger unit means a smaller number: 500 micrograms is half of 1,000 micrograms, so half a milligram. Type: 0.5 mg

paid.q: An oral solution label reads 5 mg/5 mL. A person is prescribed 3 mg. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: The label strength 5 mg/5 mL is 1 mg in each mL. Want / have x volume = 3 mg / 5 mg x 5 mL = 3 mL. Type: 3 mL

paid.q: A prefilled syringe is labelled 40 mg in 0.4 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Divide the dose by the volume: 40 mg / 0.4 mL = 100 mg per mL. Sense check: 0.4 mL is less than 1 mL, so 1 mL holds more than 40 mg. Type: 100 mg

paid.q: A full 200 mL bottle is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. The dose is 10 mL. How many doses does the full bottle contain?
paid.w: The strength is not needed: count doses by volume. 200 mL / 10 mL = 20 doses. Sense check: 20 x 10 mL = 200 mL. The question asks for a count, so no unit is typed. Type: 20

paid.q: A label reads 2 mg/mL. What volume contains 7 mg? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: "2 mg/mL" means 2 mg in each 1 mL. Want / have x volume = 7 mg / 2 mg x 1 mL = 3.5 mL. Sense check: 3.5 x 2 = 7. Type: 3.5 mL

paid.q: A client is prescribed levetiracetam oral solution 750 mg. The label reads 100 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: "100 mg/mL" means 100 mg in each mL. Want / have x volume = 750 mg / 100 mg x 1 mL = 7.5 mL. Sense check: 7.5 x 100 = 750. Type: 7.5 mL

paid.q: A client's lacosamide syrup is labelled 10 mg/mL, and the bottle holds 200 mL. How many milligrams of lacosamide are in the full bottle? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: "10 mg/mL" means 10 mg in each mL. Whole bottle: 10 mg x 200 mL = 2,000 mg. Type without a comma. Sense check: 200 lots of 10 mg. Type: 2000 mg

paid.q: A client is prescribed lamotrigine 100 mg. The tablets available contain 25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 100 mg / 25 mg = 4 tablets. Sense check: 4 x 25 mg = 100 mg. Type: 4

paid.q: A client is prescribed carbamazepine 400 mg. The stock tablets are carbamazepine 200 mg. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 400 mg / 200 mg = 2 tablets. Sense check: the dose is twice the tablet strength. Type: 2

paid.q: A client is prescribed acetazolamide 500 mg. The tablets available contain 250 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 500 mg / 250 mg = 2 tablets. Sense check: 2 x 250 mg = 500 mg. Type: 2

paid.q: A person is prescribed 1 g of a medicine. The tablets available contain 500 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Convert first so both are in mg: 1 g x 1,000 = 1,000 mg. Tablets = 1,000 mg / 500 mg = 2 tablets. Sense check: two 500 mg tablets make 1 g. Type: 2

paid.q: You have a prescription for 0.25 mg of a medicine. Each tablet contains 125 micrograms. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Convert to the same unit: 0.25 mg x 1,000 = 250 micrograms. Tablets = 250 micrograms / 125 micrograms = 2 tablets. Sense check: 125 + 125 = 250. Type: 2

paid.q: A person is prescribed 1.5 g of a medicine. The stock tablets contain 500 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Convert grams to milligrams: 1.5 g x 1,000 = 1,500 mg. Tablets = 1,500 mg / 500 mg = 3 tablets. Sense check: three 500 mg tablets make 1.5 g. Type: 3

paid.q: You have a prescription for 600 micrograms of a medicine. The tablets available contain 0.3 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Convert the tablet strength: 0.3 mg x 1,000 = 300 micrograms. Tablets = 600 micrograms / 300 micrograms = 2 tablets. Sense check: 2 x 0.3 mg = 0.6 mg = 600 micrograms. Type: 2

paid.q: A person is prescribed 7.5 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 5 mg each and are scored so they can be halved. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 7.5 mg / 5 mg = 1.5 tablets. The tablets are scored, so one and a half tablets can be given. Sense check: 5 mg + 2.5 mg = 7.5 mg. Type: 1.5

paid.q: You have a prescription for 250 micrograms of a medicine. The tablets available contain 0.5 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Convert: 0.5 mg x 1,000 = 500 micrograms. Tablets = 250 micrograms / 500 micrograms = 0.5 tablet. The tablet is scored, so half a tablet can be given. Type: 0.5

paid.q: A person is prescribed 62.5 mg of a medicine. The stock tablets contain 25 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 62.5 mg / 25 mg = 2.5 tablets. Scored tablets can be halved, so give two and a half tablets. Sense check: 25 + 25 + 12.5 = 62.5 mg. Type: 2.5

paid.q: A person is prescribed 3.75 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 2.5 mg each and are scored so they can be halved. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 3.75 mg / 2.5 mg = 1.5 tablets. Half of a 2.5 mg tablet is 1.25 mg, and 2.5 + 1.25 = 3.75 mg. Type: 1.5

paid.q: You have a prescription for 1.25 g of a medicine. The tablets available contain 500 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Convert: 1.25 g x 1,000 = 1,250 mg. Tablets = 1,250 mg / 500 mg = 2.5 tablets. The tablets are scored, so two and a half can be given. Type: 2.5

paid.q: A person is prescribed 0.5 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 1 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 0.5 mg / 1 mg = 0.5 tablet. The tablet is scored, so half a tablet can be given. Type 0.5 with the leading zero, not .5. Type: 0.5

paid.q: You have a prescription for 1.5 mg of a medicine. Each tablet contains 1 mg and is scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Tablets = want / have = 1.5 mg / 1 mg = 1.5 tablets: one whole tablet and one half of a scored tablet. Sense check: 1 mg + 0.5 mg = 1.5 mg. Type: 1.5

paid.q: A person is prescribed 500 mg of a medicine four times a day (QDS). What total dose in grams is given in 24 hours? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Daily total = dose x doses per day = 500 mg x 4 = 2,000 mg. Convert to grams: 2,000 mg / 1,000 = 2 g. Sense check: four half-gram doses make 2 g. Typed answer: 2 g

paid.q: A person is prescribed 250 mg of a medicine every 8 hours. What total dose is given in 24 hours?
paid.w: Doses per day = 24 hours / 8 hours = 3 doses. Daily total = 250 mg x 3 = 750 mg. Sense check: 8-hourly is the same as three times a day. Type: 750

paid.q: A person is prescribed 2 tablets three times a day (TDS). How many tablets are taken in 24 hours?
paid.w: Tablets per day = tablets per dose x doses per day = 2 x 3 = 6 tablets. TDS means three times a day. Type: 6

paid.q: A person is prescribed 400 mg of a medicine every 6 hours. The tablets available contain 200 mg each. How many tablets are needed in 24 hours?
paid.w: Tablets per dose = 400 mg / 200 mg = 2. Doses per day = 24 / 6 = 4. Tablets in 24 hours = 2 x 4 = 8 tablets. Sense check: 8 x 200 mg = 1,600 mg = 400 mg x 4. Type: 8

paid.q: You have a prescription for 1 g of a medicine twice a day (BD). The tablets available contain 500 mg each. How many tablets are needed in 24 hours?
paid.w: Convert: 1 g = 1,000 mg. Tablets per dose = 1,000 / 500 = 2. BD = 2 doses, so 2 x 2 = 4 tablets in 24 hours. Sense check: 4 x 500 mg = 2 g = 1 g twice. Type: 4

paid.q: A person is prescribed 5 mg of a medicine every 4 hours. What total dose is given in 24 hours?
paid.w: Doses per day = 24 hours / 4 hours = 6 doses. Daily total = 5 mg x 6 = 30 mg. Sense check: 4-hourly gives six doses in a day. Type: 30

paid.q: A client is prescribed levetiracetam 750 mg every 12 hours. What total dose in grams is given in 24 hours? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Doses per day = 24 / 12 = 2. Daily total = 750 mg x 2 = 1,500 mg. Convert: 1,500 / 1,000 = 1.5 g. Typed answer: 1.5 g

paid.q: A client living in a residential home is prescribed levetiracetam 750 mg twice a day. The tablets available contain 250 mg each. How many tablets are needed for 28 days?
paid.w: Tablets per dose = 750 / 250 = 3. Per day = 3 x 2 = 6. For 28 days = 6 x 28 = 168 tablets. Type: 168

paid.q: A client's medicines record shows 90 tablets of lamotrigine 25 mg in stock. The client is prescribed lamotrigine 50 mg twice a day. How many tablets remain after 10 days?
paid.w: Tablets per dose = 50 / 25 = 2. Per day = 2 x 2 = 4. Used in 10 days = 40. Remaining = 90 - 40 = 50 tablets. Type: 50

paid.q: A client is prescribed carbamazepine 200 mg three times a day. A supply of 63 tablets of carbamazepine 200 mg is delivered. How many days will the supply last?
paid.w: Tablets per dose = 200 / 200 = 1. Per day = 3. Days = 63 / 3 = 21 days. Sense check: 21 x 3 = 63. Type: 21

paid.q: You have a prescription for 45 mg of an oral solution. The label reads 20 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 45 mg / 20 mg x 5 mL = 2.25 x 5 = 11.25 mL. To one decimal place: 11.3 mL (the 5 rounds up). Typed answer: 11.3 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 240 mg of an oral suspension. The label reads 80 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 240 mg / 80 mg x 1 mL = 3 mL. Sense check: 3 x 80 mg = 240 mg. The stock volume here is 1 mL, not 5 mL. Typed answer: 3 mL

paid.q: A client is prescribed sodium valproate 400 mg. The oral solution is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 400 mg / 200 mg x 5 mL = 2 x 5 = 10 mL. Sense check: twice 200 mg, so twice 5 mL. Typed answer: 10 mL

paid.q: A client is prescribed lacosamide 150 mg. The syrup is labelled 10 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 150 mg / 10 mg x 1 mL = 15 mL. Sense check: 10 mg in each mL, so 150 mg needs 15 mL. Typed answer: 15 mL

paid.q: A client is prescribed phenytoin 120 mg. The oral suspension is labelled 30 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 120 mg / 30 mg x 5 mL = 4 x 5 = 20 mL. Sense check: four lots of 30 mg, so four lots of 5 mL. Typed answer: 20 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 0.5 g of an oral suspension. The label reads 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Convert first: 0.5 g x 1,000 = 500 mg. Volume = 500 mg / 250 mg x 5 mL = 2 x 5 = 10 mL. Sense check: 0.5 g is double 250 mg. Typed answer: 10 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 1.2 g of an oral suspension. The label reads 400 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Convert: 1.2 g x 1,000 = 1,200 mg. Volume = 1,200 mg / 400 mg x 5 mL = 3 x 5 = 15 mL. Sense check: three lots of 400 mg. Typed answer: 15 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 125 micrograms of an oral solution. The label reads 0.05 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Convert the label: 0.05 mg x 1,000 = 50 micrograms per mL. Volume = 125 / 50 x 1 mL = 2.5 mL. Sense check: 50 + 50 + 25 = 125 micrograms. Typed answer: 2.5 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 0.3 g of an oral solution. The label reads 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Convert: 0.3 g x 1,000 = 300 mg. Volume = 300 mg / 125 mg x 5 mL = 2.4 x 5 = 12 mL. Sense check: 300 mg is a little more than twice 125 mg, so a little more than 10 mL. Typed answer: 12 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 0.75 g of an oral suspension. The label reads 500 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Convert: 0.75 g x 1,000 = 750 mg. Volume = 750 mg / 500 mg x 5 mL = 1.5 x 5 = 7.5 mL. Typed answer: 7.5 mL

paid.q: A 15-year-old client weighing 46 kg is prescribed levetiracetam 10 mg/kg. The oral solution is labelled 100 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Dose = 10 mg x 46 kg = 460 mg. Volume = 460 mg / 100 mg x 1 mL = 4.6 mL. Sense check: 100 mg per mL, so 460 mg is just under 5 mL. Typed answer: 4.6 mL

paid.q: A 14-year-old client weighing 45 kg is prescribed lacosamide 2 mg/kg. The syrup is labelled 10 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Dose = 2 mg x 45 kg = 90 mg. Volume = 90 mg / 10 mg x 1 mL = 9 mL. Typed answer: 9 mL

paid.q: A 10-year-old client weighing 34 kg is prescribed carbamazepine 5 mg/kg. The oral liquid is labelled 100 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Dose = 5 mg x 34 kg = 170 mg. Volume = 170 mg / 100 mg x 5 mL = 1.7 x 5 = 8.5 mL. Sense check: the liquid is 20 mg in each mL, and 170 / 20 = 8.5. Typed answer: 8.5 mL

paid.q: A medicine has a stated maximum of 4 g in 24 hours. A person has already been given 2.5 g in the last 24 hours. What is the most that can still be given in this 24-hour period, in mg?
paid.w: Remaining = maximum - amount given = 4 g - 2.5 g = 1.5 g. Convert to mg: 1.5 x 1,000 = 1,500 mg. Type 1500 with no comma. Type: 1500

paid.q: A medicine has a stated maximum of 1.2 g in 24 hours. Each dose is 200 mg. What is the largest number of doses that can be given in 24 hours?
paid.w: Convert: 1.2 g x 1,000 = 1,200 mg. Doses = 1,200 mg / 200 mg = 6 doses. Sense check: 6 x 200 mg = 1,200 mg, exactly the maximum. Type: 6

paid.q: A medicine has a dose range of 10 to 15 mg/kg per dose. A person weighs 60 kg. What is the highest single dose within this range?
paid.w: The top of the range is 15 mg/kg. Highest dose = 15 mg x 60 kg = 900 mg. The lowest would be 10 x 60 = 600 mg. Type: 900

paid.q: A person is prescribed 750 mg of a medicine every 6 hours. The stated maximum is 2 g in 24 hours. By how many mg does the prescribed daily total exceed the maximum?
paid.w: Daily total = 750 mg x (24 / 6) = 750 x 4 = 3,000 mg. Maximum = 2 g = 2,000 mg. Excess = 3,000 - 2,000 = 1,000 mg. The prescription needs querying before any dose is given. Type: 1000

paid.q: A person is prescribed furosemide 30 mg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 20 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 30 mg / 20 mg x 2 mL = 1.5 x 2 = 3 mL. Sense check: the label is 10 mg in each mL, so 30 mg needs 3 mL. Type: 3 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed haloperidol 1.5 mg by subcutaneous injection. The ampoule label reads 5 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 1.5 mg / 5 mg x 1 mL = 0.3 mL. Sense check: 1.5 mg is less than a third of 5 mg, so well under 1 mL. Type: 0.3 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed ondansetron 4 mg by slow intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 8 mg in 4 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 4 mg / 8 mg x 4 mL = 0.5 x 4 = 2 mL. Sense check: the label is 2 mg in each mL, so 4 mg needs 2 mL. Type: 2 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed tramadol 75 mg by intramuscular injection. The ampoule label reads 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 75 mg / 100 mg x 2 mL = 0.75 x 2 = 1.5 mL. Sense check: 75 mg is three quarters of the ampoule, so three quarters of 2 mL. Type: 1.5 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed oxycodone 7.5 mg by slow intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 7.5 mg / 10 mg x 1 mL = 0.75 mL. Sense check: 7.5 mg is three quarters of 10 mg, so three quarters of 1 mL. Type: 0.75 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed ketorolac 10 mg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 30 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

paid.q: A person's 24-hour fluid balance chart shows a total input of 3020 mL and a total output of 2385 mL. What is the fluid balance? If the balance is a gain, put + before your answer (for example +100 mL). If it is a loss, put - before your answer (for example -100 mL). Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Balance = input - output = 3020 - 2385 = +635 mL. Input is larger, so the person has gained fluid and the answer carries a plus sign. Sense check: about 3 L in and 2.4 L out is a gain of about 600 mL. Type: +635 mL

paid.q: A person's fluid balance chart records intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL/hour, entered at 0900, 1000, 1100, 1200, 1300, 1400 (6 hourly entries). What is the total intravenous input?
paid.w: Each hourly entry at 125 mL/hour records 125 mL. There are 6 entries (0900, 1000, 1100, 1200, 1300 and 1400), so 125 x 6 = 750 mL. Sense check: 125 mL is one eighth of a litre, and six of them is three quarters of a litre. Type: 750

paid.q: A person's fluid balance chart shows intravenous 5% glucose at 83 mL/hour, entered at 0100, 0200, 0300, 0400, 0500, 0600, 0700, 0800 (8 hourly entries), then 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL/hour, entered at 0900, 1000, 1100, 1200 (4 hourly entries). What is the total intravenous input?
paid.w: First fluid: 83 mL x 8 entries = 664 mL. Second fluid: 125 mL x 4 entries = 500 mL. Total IV input = 664 + 500 = 1164 mL. Sense check: about 650 mL plus 500 mL is just over 1.1 L. Type: 1164

paid.q: A client with a learning disability is fed through a PEG. Over 24 hours the feed runs at 85 mL/hour for 16 hours. The tube is flushed with 30 mL of water before and 30 mL after the feed, and with 40 mL of water at each of 4 medicine rounds. What is the total input for the 24 hours?
paid.w: Feed: 85 mL x 16 hours = 1360 mL. Feed flushes: 30 + 30 = 60 mL. Medicine flushes: 40 x 4 = 160 mL. Total input = 1360 + 60 + 160 = 1580 mL. Sense check: flushes add about 200 mL to a feed of about 1.4 L. Type: 1580

paid.q: A client with a learning disability is fed through a PEG and is on a 24-hour fluid balance chart. paid.w: Input: feed 1500 mL + flushes 50 x 6 = 300 mL, total 1800 mL. Output: urine 400 + 350 + 350 + 400 = 1500 mL. Balance = 1800 - 1500 = +300 mL. Sense check: the flushes are what put the client in a gain. Type: +300 mL

paid.q: A client with a learning disability is prescribed 1200 mL of enteral feed through a PEG, to run on a pump over 15 hours. At what rate should the feed pump be set?
paid.w: Rate = volume / time = 1200 mL / 15 hours = 80 mL per hour. The pump box is number-only with mL per hour printed after it. Sense check: 80 x 15 = 1200, and enteral feed pumps commonly run at tens of mL per hour, so 80 is plausible. Type: 80

paid.q: You have a prescription for 9 mg. The ampoule label reads 25 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 9 / 25 x 1 = 0.36 mL. Two decimal places are asked for, and the value is below 1, so write the leading zero: 0.36 mL. Sense check: 9 mg is just over a third of 25 mg. Type: 0.36 mL

paid.q: A tablet label states a strength of 0.125 mg. How many micrograms is this?
paid.w: mg to micrograms: multiply by 1000. 0.125 x 1000 = 125 micrograms. "micrograms" is printed after the number-only box, so type only the number. Sense check: a small fraction of a mg is a few hundred micrograms or fewer. Type: 125

paid.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 1000 mL, IV, over 7 hours, start 1000. At what rate should the infusion pump be set? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
paid.w: Rate = 1000 / 7 = 142.857 mL per hour. The first dropped digit is 8 (5 or more), so round up: 143. Sense check: 143 x 7 = 1001, close to 1000. Type: 143

paid.q: You have a prescription for 35 mg. The ampoule label reads 15 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 35 / 15 x 1 = 2.333 mL. The second decimal digit is 3 (less than 5), so round down: 2.3 mL. Sense check: 35 mg is just over twice 15 mg. Type: 2.3 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 7.5 mg. The ampoule label reads 12 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 7.5 / 12 = 0.625 mL. The third decimal digit is exactly 5, which rounds up: 0.63 mL. Sense check: 7.5 mg is a little over half of 12 mg. Type: 0.63 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 750 micrograms of a medicine for nebulisation. It is supplied in 500 microgram ampoules. How many ampoules need to be opened?
paid.w: 750 / 500 = 1.5 ampoules. Part of an ampoule cannot be opened on its own, so round UP to the next whole ampoule: 2 ampoules (and discard the unused part per policy). Type: 2

paid.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 500 mL, IV, over 2 hours 45 minutes. At what rate should the infusion pump be set? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
paid.w: Convert the time first: 45 minutes = 45 / 60 = 0.75 hours, so 2 hours 45 minutes = 2.75 hours. Rate = 500 / 2.75 = 181.82 mL per hour, which rounds to 182. Sense check: 180 x 2.75 = 495. Type: 182

paid.q: You have a prescription for 85 mg. The bottle label reads 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Want / have x volume = 85 / 120 x 5 = 3.5417 mL. The third decimal digit is 1, so round down: 3.54 mL. Round only the final answer, never 85 / 120 on its own (0.71 x 5 = 3.55 is wrong). Type: 3.54 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 360 mg. The bottle label reads 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Key it in order: 360 / 120 = 3, then x 5 = 15 mL. Keying 360 / (120 x 5) gives 0.6, which is wrong. Divide first, then multiply by the stock volume. Sense check: 360 mg is three times 120 mg, so three times 5 mL. Type: 15 mL

paid.q: A person is prescribed 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride followed by 250 mL of 5% glucose, run one after the other over 6 hours in total at a constant rate. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
paid.w: Add the volumes first: 500 + 250 = 750 mL. Then divide by the time: 750 / 6 = 125 mL per hour. Press equals after the addition before dividing. Sense check: 125 x 6 = 750. Type: 125

paid.q: A person weighing 68 kg is prescribed 2.5 mg/kg of a medicine by slow IV injection. The vial label reads 50 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Step 1, dose: 2.5 x 68 = 170 mg. Step 2, volume: 170 / 50 x 2 = 6.8 mL. Write the dose on the note board before the second step so it is not lost. Sense check: 170 mg is just over three vials' worth of 50 mg. Type: 6.8 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 1 g four times a day for 5 days. The tablets are 500 mg each. How many tablets are needed for the whole course?
paid.w: Convert: 1 g = 1000 mg. Tablets per dose = 1000 / 500 = 2. Per day = 2 x 4 = 8. Course = 8 x 5 = 40 tablets. Chain it on the calculator: 1000 / 500 x 4 x 5. Sense check: 2 tablets four times a day is 8 a day. Type: 40

paid.q: You have a prescription for 0.25 mg. The tablets are 125 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Make the units match before dividing: 0.25 mg x 1000 = 250 micrograms. Tablets = 250 / 125 = 2. Dividing 0.25 by 125 without converting gives 0.002, which no dose can be. Type: 2

paid.q: A person's 24-hour fluid balance chart shows a total input of 2350 mL and a total output of 1875 mL. What is the fluid balance? If the balance is a gain, put + before your answer (for example +100 mL). If it is a loss, put - before your answer (for example -100 mL). Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Key input first, then subtract output: 2350 - 1875 = 475. Input is larger, so it is a gain: +475 mL. If you key output first the calculator shows -475; check which total is bigger before writing the sign. Type: +475 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 2 g. The tablets are 500 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
paid.w: Estimate first: 2 g is a few times 500 mg, so expect a small whole number. 2 g = 2000 mg; 2000 / 500 = 4 tablets. An answer like 0.004 or 250 fails the estimate. Type: 4

paid.q: You have a prescription for 62.5 micrograms. The ampoule label reads 250 micrograms in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Estimate: 62.5 is a quarter of 250, so a quarter of 1 mL. Want / have x volume = 62.5 / 250 x 1 = 0.25 mL. Type: 0.25 mL

paid.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 1.5 L, IV, over 12 hours, start 0600. At what rate should the infusion pump be set?
paid.w: Convert: 1.5 L = 1500 mL. Rate = 1500 / 12 = 125 mL per hour. Sense check: pump rates are usually tens to a few hundred mL per hour; 0.125 or 8 cannot run 1.5 L in 12 hours. Type: 125

paid.q: You have a prescription for 7.5 mg. The bottle label reads 2.5 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Estimate: 7.5 mg is three times 2.5 mg, so three times 5 mL. Want / have x volume = 7.5 / 2.5 x 5 = 15 mL. Answers below 5 mL fail the estimate, because the dose is more than the strength in 5 mL. Type: 15 mL

paid.q: You have a prescription for 300 mg. The ampoule label reads 150 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
paid.w: Estimate: 300 mg is two ampoules' worth, so 2 x 2 mL. Want / have x volume = 300 / 150 x 2 = 4 mL. An answer of 1 mL or 2 mL would give less than one ampoule's dose, which fails the estimate. Type: 4 mL

paid.q: A person weighing 72 kg is prescribed 0.1 mg/kg of a medicine. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
paid.w: Dose = 0.1 x 72 = 7.2 mg. Volume = 7.2 / 10 x 1 = 0.72 mL. Sense check: the dose is less than one 10 mg ampoule, so the volume must be less than 1 mL; 7.2 or 72 mL are tenfold or hundredfold errors. Type: 0.72 mL

paid.q: Part A of the CBT has 15 items in 30 minutes. On average, how many minutes are available for each item?
paid.w: Time per item = 30 minutes / 15 items = 2 minutes. Use this as a pacing guide: after 15 minutes you should be about halfway (item 7 or 8). Type: 2

paid.q: In a 30-minute numeracy test with 15 items, 18 minutes have passed and 8 items are answered. On average, how many minutes are left for each remaining item? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Time left = 30 - 18 = 12 minutes. Items left = 15 - 8 = 7. Time per item = 12 / 7 = 1.714 minutes, which is 1.7 to one decimal place. Behind the 2-minute pace, so flag slow items and keep moving. Type: 1.7

paid.q: In a 30-minute numeracy test with 15 items, you plan to keep 6 minutes at the end for review. On average, how many minutes can you spend on each item? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Working time = 30 - 6 = 24 minutes. Time per item = 24 / 15 = 1.6 minutes, about 1 minute 36 seconds. Use the review minutes to revisit flagged items and recheck signs, units and decimal places. Type: 1.6

paid.q: The pass mark for a 15-item numeracy test is 13 correct. What percentage is this? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
paid.w: Percentage = 13 / 15 x 100 = 86.67%. The first dropped digit is 6, so round up to 87%. That leaves room for two wrong answers at most, so every item deserves a quick format check. Type: 87

paid.q: A 15-item numeracy test has a pass mark of 13. What is the largest number of items that can be answered incorrectly while still passing?
paid.w: Items allowed wrong = 15 - 13 = 2. With so little margin, checking units, rounding and the answer format on every item matters as much as the arithmetic. Type: 2

paid.q: The test clock shows 7 minutes 30 seconds remaining and 4 items are unanswered. On average, how many minutes are available for each item? Write your answer to one decimal place.
paid.w: Convert: 30 seconds = 0.5 minutes, so 7 minutes 30 seconds = 7.5 minutes. Time per item = 7.5 / 4 = 1.875 minutes, which is 1.9 to one decimal place. Type: 1.9
